title: Lineage & the Microsoft stack
blurb: How lineage gets extracted from SQL Server, SSIS and Power BI, where it breaks, and how to hold a vendor to a spec.

cards.prompt: Static (design-time) vs runtime lineage: how is each captured, and what does each miss?
cards.answer: Static lineage parses definitions (view and procedure code, ETL packages, report queries) to infer dependencies. It covers paths that haven't run lately, but it misses anything built at runtime (dynamic SQL, parameterized connections) and can show paths that never execute. Runtime lineage records what actually ran (query logs, job events). It is accurate for those paths but only covers the observation window.
points: Static = parse code/definitions; runtime = observe execution
Static misses runtime-built SQL and connections
Static can include dead paths
Runtime only covers what ran in the window
cards.source: General; see OpenLineage docs for the runtime model

cards.prompt: Which SQL Server catalog view records name-based dependencies between views, procedures and functions and the objects they reference?
cards.answer: sys.sql_expression_dependencies. Its companions are the functions sys.dm_sql_referenced_entities and sys.dm_sql_referencing_entities.

cards.prompt: Why is lineage through T-SQL stored procedures hard to extract automatically? Give at least four reasons.
cards.answer: Dynamic SQL: object names live in strings assembled at runtime (EXEC, sp_executesql). Temp tables and table variables: intermediate steps aren't catalog objects. SELECT INTO and runtime DDL create objects that don't exist when the code is parsed. Deferred name resolution lets a procedure reference objects that don't exist yet. Cross-database references, linked servers (four-part names) and synonyms add indirection. Branches mean a static parser can't tell which path runs.
points: Dynamic SQL hides names in strings
Temp tables and table variables break the chain
SELECT INTO / runtime DDL create objects at execution
Deferred name resolution
Cross-database, linked-server and synonym indirection
Control flow: static parsing can't know which branch runs
cards.source: Microsoft Learn (dependency tracking, deferred name resolution); general

cards.prompt: How do catalog tools usually harvest Power BI metadata (datasets, tables, columns, measures, M and DAX, sources), and what must an admin switch on?
cards.answer: Through the Power BI/Fabric admin scanner APIs (WorkspaceInfo: PostWorkspaceInfo, GetScanStatus, GetScanResult), usually called as a service principal. Tenant settings must allow detailed metadata, and DAX and mashup expressions, in admin API responses. Otherwise scans return little more than names.
cards.why: If Power BI lineage is thin, the first question is whether those tenant settings and service-principal access are enabled.

cards.prompt: Power BI-to-SQL Server lineage often breaks at the seam even when both connectors work on their own. Why?
cards.answer: The two ends have to be stitched together by matching the source's identity. The server and database named in Power Query (alias, FQDN, IP, named instance, port, gateway) must match how the SQL Server connector registered that server. Native SQL queries embedded in Power Query also have to be parsed to know which tables they touch.
points: Cross-system lineage is an identity-resolution problem between connectors
Server name variants (alias/FQDN/IP/instance/port) break the match
Native queries in M need SQL parsing
Parameters and gateways can hide the real source

cards.prompt: Impact analysis vs root-cause analysis: which direction does each walk the lineage graph?
cards.answer: Impact analysis walks downstream: what breaks if I change this? Root-cause analysis walks upstream: where did this bad number come from?

cards.prompt: When is table-level lineage not enough?
cards.answer: When you need to know which source fields feed a specific column or measure. Examples: assessing a definition change to one field, tracing PII, or chasing one bad number back through one transformed column. Table-level lineage shows that a dependency exists. Column-level lineage shows which fields are involved and through what transformation.
points: Field-level change impact
PII tracing
Debugging a single wrong metric
Table-level shows existence; column-level shows which fields and how

cards.prompt: What is OpenLineage, and what are its three core entities?
cards.answer: An open standard (LF AI & Data Foundation) for emitting runtime lineage events from pipelines. Its core entities are Job, Run and Dataset, extended through facets.
cards.why: Marquez is the reference backend. Airflow, Spark and dbt have integrations.

cards.prompt: Where does an SSIS package keep its data-flow definition, and what defeats static parsing of it?
cards.answer: In the package XML (.dtsx). Under the project deployment model it ships inside an .ispac to the SSISDB catalog. Runtime expressions, variables and parameters defeat static parsing: dynamic connection strings, SQL built from variables, ForEach loops over files.
cards.source: Microsoft Learn: SSIS packages and deployment

cards.prompt: A vendor says 'automated lineage is supported.' Write the acceptance criteria you'd put in the statement of work.
cards.answer: Name the exact sources, versions and deployment models (on-prem SQL Server version, SSIS project deployment, Power BI service). Name the object types covered: tables, views, procedures, functions, SSIS packages, Power BI datasets and reports. State the granularity (table or column). Require end-to-end stitching across systems using your servers' real names. Supply a test fixture: a known chain from table to view to procedure to dataset to report, with the expected graph, demonstrated on your environment. Set the refresh cadence, what is automated versus manual, and the remedy if a criterion fails.
points: Exact sources, versions, deployment models
Object types in scope
Granularity: table vs column
Cross-system stitching on your real server names
A test fixture with expected graph, demonstrated on your data
Refresh cadence, manual vs automated, remedy on failure
